topic: Money and currency II — mixed tiers
description: Money supply (M0-M3), demonetisation, CBDC, currency chest

questions.stem: Which of the following forms India's 'Reserve Money' (M0)?

options.option_text: Currency with the public + demand deposits
Currency in circulation + bankers' deposits with RBI + other deposits with RBI
Fixed deposits only
Savings bank deposits

questions.explanation: M0 ('reserve money' / 'monetary base' / 'high-powered money') — the most liquid measure, what the RBI directly creates. M1 = M0 + demand deposits; M2 = M1 + post-office savings deposits; M3 = M1 + time deposits with banks ('broad money' — the most commonly reported aggregate). RBI targets broad money (M3) in its monetary policy framework.

questions.stem: India's demonetisation of ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes was announced on:

options.option_text: 8 April 2016
8 November 2016
1 July 2017
15 August 2016

questions.explanation: PM Narendra Modi announced demonetisation of the then-existing ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes on 8 November 2016, effective midnight. New ₹500 and ₹2,000 notes were introduced. The ₹2,000 note was withdrawn from circulation in May 2023. Stated objectives — counter black money, fake currency, terror financing. Impact was contested in the RBI's 2017 annual report showing that 99.3 % of the demonetised notes were returned.

questions.stem: The 'e-Rupee' launched by the RBI (pilot in 2022) is an example of:

options.option_text: Cryptocurrency
Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC)
Mobile-wallet balance
A new UPI app

questions.explanation: CBDC — central-bank-issued digital currency, legal tender, centralised. Distinct from cryptocurrency (decentralised, private, volatile). The RBI's e-Rupee (digital rupee) comes in wholesale (e₹-W, for bank-to-bank settlement, pilot Nov 2022) and retail (e₹-R, for consumers, pilot Dec 2022) variants. China (e-CNY), Nigeria (e-Naira), Bahamas (Sand Dollar) are other early CBDC adopters.

questions.stem: Coins in India are minted by:

options.option_text: The Reserve Bank of India
The Government of India (through SPMCIL)
Commercial banks
State governments

questions.explanation: Coins are minted under the Coinage Act 2011 by the Security Printing and Minting Corporation of India Ltd (SPMCIL) — under the Ministry of Finance. Four mints: Mumbai, Kolkata, Hyderabad, Noida. The RBI distributes them and also has the sole right to ISSUE currency notes (printed at currency presses in Nashik, Dewas + BRBNMPL presses in Mysuru and Salboni).

questions.stem: The 'money multiplier' of an economy is approximately the reciprocal of:

options.option_text: The repo rate
The cash reserve ratio (CRR)
The bank rate
The inflation rate

questions.explanation: Basic money-multiplier model — if banks keep fraction 'r' (CRR) of deposits as reserves and lend the rest, the total money created from a new deposit is 1/r. If CRR = 4 %, the multiplier is 25 (ignoring other leakages like cash in hand). Real-world multipliers are lower due to cash preferences, excess reserves, and the SLR constraint. Still the simplest link between reserve ratio and broad-money growth.

questions.stem: 'Gresham's law' in monetary economics states that:

options.option_text: High taxes drive out investment
Bad money drives out good money from circulation
Too much money causes inflation
Savings rise with interest rates

questions.explanation: Gresham's law (attributed to Sir Thomas Gresham, 16th c.) — 'Bad money drives out good' — when two currencies circulate at the same legal value but have different intrinsic values, people hoard the more valuable (good) one and spend the less valuable (bad) one. Classic case — when debased silver coins circulated alongside pure silver coins, pure ones disappeared from daily use.

questions.stem: The 'rupee' symbol ₹ — adopted by India in 2010 — was designed by:

options.option_text: A British graphic designer
D. Udaya Kumar (IIT Bombay professor)
The Reserve Bank of India
The Mint of India

questions.explanation: D. Udaya Kumar, a post-graduate from IIT Bombay's Industrial Design Centre, won the Government's open design competition in 2010; his ₹ glyph — a stylised fusion of the Devanagari letter 'र' (ra) and the Latin 'R', with two horizontal lines at top — was adopted by the Union Cabinet on 15 July 2010. Unicode code point U+20B9. India is one of the few countries whose currency symbol was picked via public competition.

questions.stem: The one-rupee note in India does NOT bear the signature of the RBI Governor. Instead, whose signature appears on it?

options.option_text: Governor of the Reserve Bank of India
Finance Secretary, Government of India
Union Finance Minister of India
Chairman of the Finance Commission

questions.explanation: The ₹1 note is issued by the Ministry of Finance (not the RBI) and therefore bears the Finance Secretary's signature. All higher denomination notes are RBI liabilities and carry the RBI Governor's signature. The Finance Minister does not sign currency; the Finance Secretary is the authorised signatory for the ₹1 note.

questions.stem: Which of the following instruments is classified as 'near money' (quasi-money) in monetary economics?

options.option_text: Currency notes issued by the Reserve Bank of India
Fixed deposits held in scheduled commercial banks
Demand deposits in current accounts at banks
Cash reserves held by banks with the RBI

questions.explanation: Near money refers to highly liquid non-cash assets that can quickly be converted to money but are not directly spendable — fixed deposits are the classic example. Currency notes and demand deposits are already part of M1 (active money). Cash reserves with the RBI are part of M0 (reserve money), not a quasi-money instrument held by the public.

questions.stem: According to Fisher's equation of exchange (MV = PT), if the money supply doubles while velocity of circulation and real output both remain constant, what happens to the general price level?

options.option_text: Remain unchanged due to output neutralising the money effect
Double, as the quantity theory predicts proportional inflation
Halve, because more money reduces the value of transactions
Rise by 50%, reflecting partial adjustment in the real economy

questions.explanation: MV = PT rearranges to P = MV/T. With V and T constant, doubling M exactly doubles P — the classical quantity theory result. Option A misunderstands the role of T: constant output does not neutralise price change, it ensures P bears the full adjustment. Option D (50% rise) would only apply if M rose by 50%, not doubled.

questions.stem: In monetary economics, 'seigniorage' specifically refers to which of the following?

options.option_text: The fee charged by banks for inter-bank fund transfers
The profit a government earns from issuing currency above its cost
The penalty levied on banks for failing to maintain CRR norms
The reserve requirement maintained by the central bank overnight

questions.explanation: Seigniorage is the difference between the face value of currency and the cost of producing and distributing it — a revenue source for the sovereign authority. For example, printing a ₹500 note costs a few rupees, yielding ~₹497 in seigniorage. Options C and D describe CRR-related tools, which are monetary policy instruments, not revenue concepts.

questions.stem: The term 'hot money' in international finance and balance-of-payments analysis refers to capital that:

options.option_text: Is physically transported across borders in the form of currency notes
Moves quickly across borders exploiting short-term interest rate gaps
Is laundered through offshore jurisdictions to avoid domestic taxation
Is held by central banks as emergency foreign-exchange reserve buffer

questions.explanation: Hot money is speculative short-term capital that flows rapidly between countries seeking higher interest rates or returns, making exchange rates and capital accounts highly volatile. Option C describes black money or money laundering — a separate concept. Option D describes official forex reserves, which are stable long-term holdings, the opposite of hot money.

questions.stem: At the 1944 Bretton Woods Conference, John Maynard Keynes proposed 'Bancor' as which of the following?

options.option_text: A fixed gold reserve ratio for all member countries of the IMF
A supranational currency for clearing international trade imbalances
A special credit facility for developing nations to access IMF loans
An international gold-exchange standard anchored to the US dollar

questions.explanation: Keynes proposed Bancor as an international unit of account, managed by a proposed International Clearing Union, to settle trade surpluses and deficits between nations without gold transfers — penalising both chronic surplus and deficit countries. The US rejected this in favour of a dollar-gold standard (Option D), which was what Bretton Woods actually adopted. Option C conflates Bancor with IMF lending facilities.

questions.stem: The 'Triffin Dilemma' (1960) exposes a fundamental contradiction in the global reserve-currency role. Which statement best captures this paradox?

options.option_text: Running surpluses builds credibility but starves global markets of reserve currency
Running deficits supplies liquidity but erodes reserve-currency confidence over time
Raising interest rates attracts capital inflows but dampens domestic growth
Pegging to gold ensures stability but prevents exchange-rate adjustment

questions.explanation: Robert Triffin argued that the US, as issuer of the world's reserve currency, had to run current-account deficits to supply global dollar liquidity — but sustained deficits would eventually undermine confidence in the dollar's gold convertibility, a self-defeating trap. Option A reverses the mechanism: surpluses would maintain credibility but starve the world of dollars, not solve the dilemma. Option C is a separate monetary-policy trilemma, not the Triffin paradox.
